477.title: Your mother's eyes
477.hook: We returned you to your mother so her eyes might be cooled (20:40)
477.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a lesson in trust and in God's care for mothers; the phrase qurrat 'ayn, coolness of the eye, is common in Muslim speech and in the du'a of 25:74 for spouses and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umar hears Ta-Ha, and a sister's courage. Your line was the page changed him.

Musa is standing in a sacred valley, barefoot, having just been told he's a prophet and sent to Pharaoh. He asks for help: his brother Harun beside him, a tongue that speaks more easily. And God, before sending him, does something tender. He reminds Musa of his own story, from before Musa could remember anything. A baby, a box, a river. And a mother on the riverbank, watching it float away.

Pharaoh was killing the baby boys of the Children of Israel. Ta-Ha says God inspired Musa's mother: put him in a chest, and put the chest in the river. The river will throw it onto the bank, and an enemy of Mine and his will take him. To save your child, let him go, toward the very palace that wants him dead. Another surah, Al-Qasas, says her heart was left empty, and she nearly gave the secret away. Then, verse thirty-nine: I cast love on you from Me, so you'd be raised under My eye. The baby is taken into Pharaoh's house and loved there. But he won't nurse from any woman they bring. His sister, who has been following the chest along the bank, steps forward and says, in Pickthall's words, "Shall I show you one who will nurse him?" Then verse forty: "and We restored thee to thy mother that her eyes might be refreshed and might not sorrow." In Arabic, kay taqarra 'aynuha: so that her eye might be cooled. Coolness of the eye is an old Arabic way of saying deep joy and relief. One explanation in the classical dictionaries: tears of grief are hot, and tears of joy are cool. The Qur'an uses the phrase elsewhere too, in a prayer for spouses and children who are a coolness of the eyes. So God, sending Musa to face Pharaoh, reminds him: you were saved, and brought back, and the reason given is a mother's grief. Before the miracles and the staff and the sea, there was a woman by a river, and God did not leave her crying.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a mother, your own, a grandmother, a friend with a new baby, a woman who mothered you though she wasn't your mother, or one who's grieving a child, and picture her face. What is she carrying right now that could be lightened, even a little? If she's died, you can think of something kind to do in her name, and if you pray, you can pray for her.

Your line: so she would not grieve. Cool eyes are eyes at rest. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.

478.title: Increase me in knowledge
478.hook: say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge (20:114)
478.howItsDone: Muslims say rabbi zidni 'ilma, from 20:114, before studying, teaching or exams, and it can be seen written up in classrooms in Muslim communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musa, returned to his mother on the riverbank. Your line was so she would not grieve.

A student in the front row writes so fast to catch every word that half of what's said slips past. The pen is ahead of the understanding. The commentators, drawing on a hadith, describe something like it in the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: when the angel Jibril brought a passage, he would repeat each word as it came, hurrying, afraid of losing one. Ta-Ha has a verse for that moment. It tells him not to hurry, and then gives him words to ask with.

Verse one hundred fourteen begins with praise: exalted is God, the true King. Then: don't hurry with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is complete. Al-Qiyamah says it more vividly: don't move your tongue to rush it; We will gather it and recite it for you. The knowledge is safe; you can breathe. And then, in Pickthall's words: "and say: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." In Arabic: rabbi zidni 'ilma. Some commentators count this as the one place in the Qur'an where the Prophet is told to ask for more of something. Not more wealth, not more time, not more followers. More knowledge. And 'ilm in the Qur'an is wide. It's knowledge of God first, but it also takes in understanding, discernment, knowing how things work and how to live. Tradition says the first word revealed to him was iqra': read, recite. Here, years later, the request is: more. A hadith in Ibn Majah and Tirmidhi preserves a prayer of his that builds on the verse: he asked God to make what he'd learned useful, to teach him what would be useful, and to increase him in knowledge. That's the balance: don't rush what's coming, and keep asking for more. Some Muslim students say rabbi zidni 'ilma before they study, before an exam, before opening a book. Six words in English. Three in Arabic.

479.title: Before sunrise and sunset
479.hook: be patient and glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130)
479.howItsDone: Muslims pray Fajr before sunrise and 'Asr before sunset among the five daily prayers, and some recite the morning and evening adhkar, including subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, at the two ends of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ilm, knowledge, and a prayer to be given more of it. Your line was rabbi zidni 'ilma. Today, our last day in Ta-Ha.

A day has two edges. The first few minutes after you wake, before the world gets in. And the last stretch of afternoon light, when the shadows go long. Everything else sits in between. Near its end, Ta-Ha tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who is hearing hard words from his opponents, what to do at both edges. It starts with patience.

Verse one hundred thirty, in Pickthall's words: bear with what they say, "and celebrate the praises of thy Lord ere the rising of the sun and ere the going down thereof." The verb is sabbih: glorify, say subhan Allah, God is far above every fault. That's tasbih, the same root as the opening of Al-Isra, glory to Him who carried His servant by night. The verse adds more times: some hours of the night, and the ends of the day. Like the dawn verse in Al-Isra a couple of weeks back, commentators read it as a map of the prayer times. Before sunrise is Fajr. Before sunset is 'Asr, the afternoon prayer. The hours of the night hold Maghrib and 'Isha. A hadith in Sahih Muslim singles out the two edges: the Prophet said that whoever prays before the rising of the sun and before its setting will not enter the Fire. Then the verse gives a reason, la'allaka tarda: so that you may be content, well pleased. That's the surprise. The command ends not in duty or reward, but in contentment. The man being mocked is told: glorify at both ends of the day, and you'll find peace. Beyond the prayers, some Muslims keep morning and evening remembrances, the adhkar, short phrases said as the day opens and as it closes. One of the simplest, from a hadith in Bukhari: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, glory to God and praise to Him. Ta-Ha opened by saying the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out. It closes by framing the day with praise at both edges, so the middle, with all its hard words, can be borne.

segments.voice: Wherever you are in your day, sit and say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath: subhan Allah. If you're not Muslim, sit with the plain meaning: glory beyond anything I can name. Then picture the two edges ahead, this evening's last light and tomorrow's first minutes, and let the word wait there for them.
Tasbih. Glorifying God at the two edges of the day, with patience in between, so that you may be content. Today's word.

480.title: Every living thing from water
480.hook: We made every living thing from water (21:30)
480.tomorrow: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
480.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu with water before prayer, and some follow the Prophet's practice of saying bismillah and drinking in three sips while seated; 21:30 is often cited when teaching care for water.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tasbih, glory to God at both edges of the day. Your line was glory at both edges. Today, a new surah.

Turn on a tap and fill a glass. It takes three seconds, and where water is cheap it costs almost nothing, so it's easy to forget what's in your hand. Leave a plant without it and it droops. Go without it yourself and you won't last long. Surah twenty-one, Al-Anbiya, the Prophets, stops in the middle of a long argument about God on a short line about what's in that glass.

Al-Anbiya is named for the prophets; it walks through many of them, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus and more. But first, it points at the world. Verse thirty, in Pickthall's words: "Have not those who disbelieve known that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, then We parted them, and we made every living thing of water?" And it ends: will they not then believe? A question, then a sign, then another question. It isn't a lecture. It asks people to look at what's already in front of them. Some modern readers connect the verse with what biology says about water and life; other scholars caution against reading the Qur'an as a science textbook, since its purpose here is a sign that leads to faith. Both are said within the tradition. What the verse plainly says: life comes from water, and water comes from God. A verse in An-Nur says God created every animal from water: some go on their bellies, some on two legs, some on four. In Muslim practice, water comes before prayer: wudu, washing the hands, mouth, nose, face and arms, wiping the head, washing the feet. And a hadith in Abu Dawud says Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Water isn't meant to be hoarded. So one line holds three things at once: a sign of the Creator, a gift to all living things, and a trust to be shared. The glass from the tap is all three.

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one, and think back along its road: rain, a river or a reservoir, pipes, the tap. Muslim custom, drawn from hadith, is to say bismillah before drinking and to drink in three sips, sitting down; if you'd like, try that. Then sit with the empty glass, and let the thanks be wordless.

481.title: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
481.hook: a flock ruins a field, and Sulayman is given the better understanding (21:78–79)
481.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 21:78–79 when teaching that judges may differ and revise rulings, and that both the careful judge who errs and the one who is right are rewarded; teachers also use it to show respect for the young.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wudu, and every living thing made of water. Your line was from water, life.

A farmer walks out to his field one morning, and it's gone. Not stolen. Eaten. Overnight, someone's flock wandered in and grazed it down to the dirt: a season's work, a family's food. The farmer goes to the king for justice. The king is Dawud, a prophet famous for his wisdom. Sitting beside him is his son, Sulayman, still young. Al-Anbiya tells the case in two verses.

The Qur'an gives the bare outline: Dawud and Sulayman judging about the field, when the people's sheep grazed it by night, and We were witness to their judgment. Then, in Pickthall's words: "And We made Solomon to understand (the case); and unto each of them We gave judgment and knowledge." Commentators, drawing on reports from companions like Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, fill in the details. Dawud ruled first: the sheep go to the owner of the field, as payment for the loss. Fair enough. Then Sulayman, some reports say he was about eleven, suggested another way. Let the farmer keep the sheep for a while and live off their milk and wool, while the shepherd works the field until it grows back to what it was. Then each takes back his own. Nobody loses everything, and the harm is actually repaired. Dawud agreed, and changed his ruling. Now the second half of the verse: to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. The Qur'an doesn't shame the father. Both were wise; on this case, the younger saw further. A hadith in Bukhari tells of a judge who works hard to reach the right ruling: if he's right, he gets two rewards, and if he's wrong, still one. Another hadith in Bukhari has the two of them again: two women claim one baby, Dawud gives it to the elder, and Sulayman calls for a knife to divide it. The younger woman cries out, give it to her, and he knows she's the mother. In both stories the younger one sees further, and in the field case, a father listens and lets his son be right.

segments.voice: Think of a problem you're working on, at home, at work, in your community, and of someone younger who knows something about it: a child, a niece, a new coworker, a student. Picture asking them what they'd do, and really listening, the way Dawud listened. What might they see that you've stopped noticing?
Sulayman. The young son whose ruling about the grazed field showed deeper wisdom than his father's, and which his father accepted. Today's word.
Your line: the young one saw it. Wisdom doesn't always wait for age. Day four hundred eighty-one, done.

482.title: Ayyub's call
482.hook: Ayyub calls, harm has touched me and You are the most merciful, and is healed (21:83–84)
482.carry: harm touched me; you are merciful
482.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayyub's words from 21:83 in times of illness or hardship, often in Arabic, as a short personal supplication alongside the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sulayman and the grazed field, where a father let his son be right. Your line was the young one saw it.

Some prayers are long, with openings and closings and lists. The one in today's verse has two parts, and neither is a request in so many words. A man has lost his health and his family, and commentators add his wealth too. They say the trial went on for years; nobody can tell you exactly how many. When he finally speaks to God about it, he doesn't argue or bargain. He says what happened, and he says who God is. Al-Anbiya keeps it to two verses. Today, the call of Ayyub, the man the Bible calls Job.
screen: `TWO PARTS: WHAT HAPPENED, WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall gives his words this way: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic it's short enough to hold in one breath. Massaniya ad-durr: harm has touched me. The verb massa means to touch. He doesn't say harm crushed me. He says it touched me, which some commentators read as courtesy, a man choosing his words carefully even in pain. Then: wa anta arhamu r-rahimin, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Notice what's missing. There is no heal me. He lays the wound next to the mercy and leaves the rest to God. The next verse says God answered. The harm was removed, and his family given back to him, with the like of them besides, as a mercy and a reminder. Surah Sad adds a little: he is told to strike the ground with his foot, and there is cool water to wash in and drink. And God calls him patient, an excellent servant. That's the surprise. The Qur'an praises Ayyub's patience in the same story where he tells God plainly that he's hurting. So patience here isn't silence. Ya'qub says something close in Surah Yusuf: he takes his grief to God and to no one else. Some scholars draw a line: complaining about God to people is one thing; telling God is part of the prayer. You may have heard longer tales of Ayyub, with details of his illness and his wife. Those are stories people tell, from later collections. The Qur'an itself stays brief.

segments.voice: Find one thing that hurts right now, a worry, a loss, a body that aches, and give it a few plain words, the way Ayyub did, without explaining or arguing. If you pray, you can say his line, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful, and stop there. If you don't, name the hurt to yourself, kindly, and let it sit beside you.
Ayyub's call. Two parts: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Named, not argued. Today's word.

483.title: Zakariyya: don't leave me alone
483.hook: my Lord, don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors (21:89)
483.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Zakariyya's prayer from 21:89 when hoping for children, and some use it more widely when asking not to be left alone; it is said quietly, as a personal supplication.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ayyub's call, harm named next to God's mercy. Your line was harm touched me; you are merciful. Today ends the week.

An old man prays in the sanctuary. His bones have grown weak, he says, and his head is ablaze with white hair. His wife is barren. He has been looking after a girl named Maryam, and whenever he goes in to her he finds food with her, and she tells him it is from God. And there, watching her, he speaks. Surah Maryam says he called to his Lord with a hidden call, a prayer said low, almost in secret. Today, Zakariyya.

Al-Anbiya gives his prayer in one verse. Pickthall: "My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors." The Arabic is la tadharni fardan. Fard means single, one alone, so the plainest sense is: don't leave me alone. Pickthall renders it childless, and that is the sense: no son, no one to carry on the work after him. But the word underneath is lonelier. Then the second half: You are the best of inheritors. In the same breath that he asks for an heir, he admits that God inherits everything in the end anyway. He's asking and letting go at once. Ayyub, yesterday, named his pain and God's mercy. Zakariyya names his fear and God's lasting. The next verse says: so We answered him, and gave him Yahya, and made his wife fit for him. The Qur'an doesn't stop at the family. It says these prophets used to hurry toward good deeds, and called on God in longing and in fear, and were humble before Him. In Surah Maryam, he asks for a sign that it's real, and is told he will not speak to people for three nights, though he is well. So the man whose prayer was a whisper gets an answer he has to carry in silence. Commentators point out where the prayer started: watching Maryam, a young girl provided for in ways no one could explain. Seeing God give to someone else is what made him brave enough to ask for himself.
screen: `LA TADHARNI FARDAN.` · `ALONE: LONELIER THAN CHILDLESS.` · `GOD, THE BEST OF INHERITORS.` · `YAHYA, AND THREE SILENT NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Notice whether there's a loneliness you've stopped mentioning, even to yourself: a friend you lost touch with, a home that's too quiet, a hope set down years ago; or think of someone else who is alone right now. If you pray, you can use Zakariyya's words, my Lord, don't leave me alone, for yourself or for them. If you don't, just hold that person in mind for a while.
Zakariyya. The old servant of the sanctuary who asked, in secret, not to be left alone, and was given Yahya. Today's word.
Your line: don't leave me alone. A prayer can ask and let go in the same breath. A week, done.
